name: The Go Engineer v3 — README Contracts

architectural_decision.core_rule: Optimize for learner progression, zero magic, rigorous proof of understanding, production-grade documentation, and job readiness without template slop or artificial over-engineering.
architectural_decision.decision: Authoritative v3 modular curriculum engineered around a zero-magic phase-based path from foundational Go to production software engineering.
architectural_decision.full_bundle_policy: Split files are authoritative. curriculum.v3.full.generated.json is an optional generated snapshot for review/export only.
architectural_decision.manifest_policy: Authoritative modular v3 manifests are the active source of truth for the curriculum engine.
architectural_decision.v2_policy: curriculum.v2.json is archived legacy import data, not the active source of truth.

contracts.purpose: World-class teaching README for a concept, systems technique, or operational skill.
contracts.applies_when: The concept is required for the core path and every learner must master it before advancing.
contracts.anti_overengineering_policy: Do not force all 17 headings if a lesson's subject matter does not warrant them. Non-applicable sections should be omitted rather than populated with placeholder slop. Always respect the item's content_contract flags (visual_model_required, machine_view_required, production_notes_required, runnable_required, tests_required).

concept.description: Deep programming fundamentals, type semantics, memory mechanics, and runtime structures.
conditional_additions: Visual model (when memory layout, pointer indirection, or headers are involved)
Production notes (when production failure modes exist)
acceptable_omissions: Debugging walkthrough (if concept is purely foundational syntax without runtime crash traps)

operations.description: Systems programming, Linux processes, signals, Docker containerization, CI/CD, and runbooks.
conditional_additions: Visual model (when process tree, network socket, or pipeline topology is involved)
Debugging walkthrough (when operational failure triage is taught)
acceptable_omissions: Performance implications (when teaching process management, signals, or configuration files)

architecture.description: Service boundaries, package structure, domain invariants, and design patterns.
conditional_additions: Go example (when architectural interface contracts are shown)
acceptable_omissions: Debugging walkthrough (for purely conceptual architectural tradeoffs and boundary definitions)
Performance implications (unless teaching sharding, latency budgets, or multi-tenant scaling)

career.description: Portfolio strategy, technical documentation, resume projects, code review preparation, and interview readiness.
acceptable_omissions: Under the hood (purely non-runtime strategic topics)
Visual model (unless illustrating project portfolio timelines)
Go example (when teaching portfolio documentation or interview communication)

debugging.description: Delve debugger drills, pprof profiling, race detector diagnostics, and panic trace recovery.

testing.description: Unit testing, table-driven tests, subtests, mocks, test harnesses, and coverage analysis.
acceptable_omissions: Performance implications (unless teaching benchmarking or memory allocation tracking)

section_specifications.Learning objective: Measurable, behavioral statement: 'By the end of this lesson, you will be able to...'
section_specifications.Why this matters: Operational and architectural justification: real-world production incidents and system design tradeoffs.
section_specifications.Mental model: Durable physical analogy or conceptual construct that accurately models mechanical behavior without hand-waving.
section_specifications.Core idea: Concise formulation of the fundamental rule, syntax, or language invariant in plain language.
section_specifications.Visual model: Concrete, domain-specific Mermaid diagram (sequenceDiagram, flowchart TD/LR, stateDiagram-v2, erDiagram) or ASCII layout. Skip if the concept has no spatial, memory, or concurrent structure.
section_specifications.Under the hood: Mechanical explanation: compiler actions, runtime structs, memory allocation, bits & bytes, adhering to the 6 Physical Pillars. Skip for pure career/strategy lessons.
section_specifications.How Go uses it: Idiomatic usage patterns across the Go standard library, runtime internals, and production architectures.
section_specifications.Go example: Complete, self-contained, runnable code (package main, imports, func main()) demonstrating the concept. Skip for text-only strategy lessons.
section_specifications.Step-by-step execution: Numbered chronological walkthrough tracing variable states, registers, stack frames, and outputs across execution.
section_specifications.Common mistakes: Markdown table format (Mistake | Why it happens | Fix) documenting real mistakes observed in production code.
section_specifications.Debugging walkthrough: Realistic failure scenario: error symptoms, Delve commands, stack traces, root cause isolation, and resolution.
section_specifications.Production notes: Operational risks, defense-in-depth patterns, and failure modes from curriculum/failures.json.
section_specifications.Performance implications: Algorithmic complexity (Big-O), heap vs stack allocations, CPU cache line effects, struct alignment, and GC overhead. Skip if performance is neutral or non-applicable.
section_specifications.Practice task: Actionable, hands-on modification exercise for the learner to alter code and observe behavioral changes.
section_specifications.Tests / verification: Exact verification commands (go run, go test -v, go test -race) and verified output signatures.
section_specifications.Review questions: 4-5 diagnostic and conceptual questions evaluating mechanical comprehension.
section_specifications.NEXT UP: Relative link and canonical item ID to the next sequential learning node in path.core.json.

status_levels.placeholder: Heading scaffold only. No substantive content.
status_levels.draft: Content written but not reviewed for quality or production realism.
status_levels.reviewed: Content reviewed by a senior engineer for technical accuracy.
status_levels.golden: Content passes all validator quality rules, satisfies the 6 Physical Pillars, and has been tested with learners.

zero_magic_enforcement.promotion_policy: A lesson may only be promoted to golden after: (1) passing validate-no-placeholder-zm with semantic checks enabled, (2) being reviewed by a senior engineer, (3) containing a real production example and real debugging scenario where applicable, (4) grounding concepts mechanically in the 6 Physical Pillars without template filler.
zero_magic_enforcement.regression_policy: Any lesson that fails a semantic quality check must be immediately reverted to draft status regardless of previous promotion.

validation_rules: Every README must match its declared contract_id and satisfy its core_required_headings without exception.
Generated sections must be marked with curriculum generated comments (<!-- curriculum:generated:start --> and <!-- curriculum:generated:end -->).
Human-written sections must not be overwritten or modified by generator scripts.
Anti-slop rule: Do not force contextual headings if the subject matter does not warrant them. Omit non-applicable sections rather than populating them with artificial template filler.
No implemented lesson may keep placeholder zero-magic text (e.g. 'mechanically without understanding', 'one step in the learner's path').
No README may use stale legacy navigation labels or non-existent lesson IDs unless inside historical migration notes.
Every future concept must use an explicit preview-only reference; lessons cannot assume mastery of unintroduced concepts.
Every project README must expose its rubric with explicit percentage weights summing to 100%.
Every module README must expose its completion checklist and sequential module arc.

No README with zero_magic_status=golden may contain template-style phrases: 'Think of X as a contract', 'X is similar to', 'in simple terms', 'basically', 'just', 'obviously', or empty analogy filler.
Every lesson README marked golden must contain at least one concrete production failure example from curriculum/failures.json in the 'Production notes' section when production failure modes apply.
Every lesson README marked golden must include a realistic debugging scenario in 'Debugging walkthrough' when error modes or debugging mechanics are taught.

Mental model sections must describe the physical mechanism, not merely restate the dictionary definition — 'A goroutine is...' is a definition; 'When you write go f(), the runtime allocates a 2 KB stack and registers the g pointer...' is a mental model.

Under the hood sections must describe what the CPU, OS, and Go runtime actually do (stack vs heap, descriptors, word boundaries, syscalls), adhering strictly to the 6 Physical Pillars for all lessons introducing runtime mechanics.
Common mistakes sections must list real mistakes observed in production code with concrete fixes, formatted as a markdown table.

Every golden lesson introducing Go primitives, memory layouts, or runtime mechanisms must ground concepts in the 6 Physical Pillars (bytes/word alignment, composite headers, concurrency engine descriptors, hash table bucket topology, CPU cache lines, or I/O buffer mechanics).

Visual models must use semantic Mermaid diagram types (flowchart TD/LR, sequenceDiagram, stateDiagram-v2, or erDiagram) with quoted labels to visualize state transitions, pointer indirection, and concurrency flows without rendering errors.

Execution and memory timelines must adhere to the discrete temporal format (T0, T1, T2...) detailing physical register, stack frame, and heap allocation states across time when temporal or concurrent flow is introduced.
All project and service capstone starters must enforce 3-tier clean domain separation (transport/ -> domain/ -> repo/) with domain layers free of external framework dependencies.

Cognitive load budgeting: each lesson may introduce at most 1 primary new concept; all prerequisite language constructs must be verified against curriculum/crossrefs.json and curriculum/concepts.json.
Transitive prerequisite verification: concepts must strictly follow canonical introduction in curriculum/concepts.json; preview locations must strictly precede, reinforcement must strictly follow.
